Customers – The system can provide customers with a more reliable service experience through automated status updates at key transaction points rather than requiring them to message for progress inquiries. Theory of Non-relational Database Management System

The theoretical framework of Non-relational Database Management Systems (NoSQL) is primarily rooted in the CAP Theorem and a shift toward flexible data modeling to address the limitations of traditional relational systems in handling Big Data.

NoSQL database theory is centered on the CAP Theorem, which states that distributed systems must balance three competing needs: consistency, availability, and partition tolerance (Oprea et al., 2023). To achieve high availability and the ability to "scale out" across multiple servers, NoSQL systems often swap strict, real-time consistency for eventual consistency (Oprea et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2017). Unlike traditional databases with rigid structures, NoSQL uses a schema-on-read approach, allowing data to be stored in flexible formats like Key-Value pairs, documents, columns, or graphs (Klettke et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2017). This flexibility enables lazy schema evolution, where data is updated only when needed, making it ideal for handling massive amounts of unstructured "Big Data" (Klettke et al., 2016). While this provides great speed and agility, it can make complex queries difficult, leading many modern researchers to use hybrid models that combine NoSQL’s scalability with the reliability of traditional SQL systems (Sen & Mukherjee, 2023; Wu et al., 2017).
